1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 51-year-old woman with a chief complaint of "chest tightness and shortness of breath for 4 days, worsened for 2 days." Four days before admission, after exposure to cold, she developed chest tightness and shortness of breath, which worsened after activity. Two days earlier, the symptoms worsened; she was unable to lie flat at night and needed to sit leaning forward to rest. At an outside hospital, troponin was 154 pg/ml↑; arterial blood gas analysis showed pCO2 54 mmHg↑, pO2 85 mmHg; chest X-ray showed pleural thickening, and she was diagnosed with "shortness of breath, cause to be investigated: pulmonary embolism? heart failure?" Diuretic, vasodilator, and ventilatory support treatment was given without improvement. She had a history of snoring, intermittent sleep apnea, hypertension for more than 10 years, and prior hysterectomy. On admission physical examination: temperature 36.8℃, pulse 103/min, respirations 36/min, blood pressure 140/78 mmHg, pulse oxygen saturation 97%, overweight body habitus, acute ill appearance, slightly decreased breath sounds in both lungs, no dry or moist rales, and no pleural friction rub. Cardiac dullness was not enlarged, heart rate 103/min, regular rhythm, and no pathologic murmur was heard in any valve area. The abdomen was full; the liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margin; shifting dullness was negative; there was no edema of either lower extremity. Laboratory and ancillary examinations were as follows: after presentation to our emergency department on Day -1, complete blood count showed WBC 18.35×10^9/L, N 78.4%, HB 161 g/L, PLT 409×10^9/L; inflammatory markers: PCT 0.11 ng/ml; ESR 20 mm/h; liver and kidney function: ALT 67.2 IU/L, AST 35.6 IU/L, BUN 6.18 mmol/L, Cr 42.1 umol/L; TNT 109.7 pg/ml; CK 346.1 u/l, CK-MB 39.6 u/l; BNP 63 pg/ml; blood glucose 9.4 mmol/L; arterial blood gas analysis: pH 7.29, pCO2 76 mmHg↑, pO2 154 mmHg, HCO3- 36.4 mmol/l↑; abdominal ultrasonography: fatty liver, status post hysterectomy. Electrocardiogram (Figure 1): sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy, nonspecific ST-T changes; chest CT (Figure 2): multiple linear increased-density opacities were seen in both lungs, with slightly indistinct margins, and small amounts of ground-glass opacities in both lower lungs. Infectious lesions were considered; clinical correlation was recommended.

differential_diagnoses.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome with obstructive sleep apnea, resulting in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure
supporting_evidence: History of snoring and intermittent sleep apnea
Overweight body habitus

Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.29, pCO2 76 mmHg↑, HCO3- 36.4 mmol/l↑, indicating marked hypercapnia with compensation, consistent with acute exacerbation on the basis of chronic hypoventilation
Chief complaint: chest tightness and shortness of breath, and “unable to lie flat at night, requiring a seated forward-leaning position to rest,” indicating a marked increase in work of breathing.

Physical examination: breath sounds in both lungs were slightly decreased, with no dry or moist rales or pleural friction rub heard, which is more supportive of hypoventilation rather than typical consolidation or obvious pulmonary edema.
Pulse oxygen saturation 97%, but with concomitant severe CO2 retention, indicating relatively preserved oxygenation with prominent ventilatory impairment.
opposing_evidence: Chest CT showed "multiple linear areas of increased density in both lungs with slightly indistinct margins, and a small amount of ground-glass opacity in both lower lungs. Infectious lesion is considered," indicating that, in addition to hypoventilation, pulmonary parenchymal lesions may also coexist.
WBC 18.35×10^9/L, N 78.4%, evidence of infection or a stress response is present; the entire acute exacerbation cannot be explained solely by sleep-related hypoventilation

differential_diagnoses.name: Community-acquired pulmonary infection (including atypical pneumonia/bronchopneumonia) with precipitated respiratory failure
supporting_evidence: Before disease onset, the patient had chest tightness and shortness of breath after catching a cold.
CBC: WBC 18.35×10^9/L, N 78.4%, suggesting possible inflammation or infection

Chest CT (Figure 2) and the written description showed "multiple linear hyperdense opacities in both lungs, with slightly indistinct margins, and a small amount of ground-glass opacity in both lower lungs," and explicitly stated "infectious lesion is considered; clinical correlation is recommended."
Respiratory rate 36 breaths/min, indicating severe acute respiratory system involvement
A small amount of ground-glass opacity in both lower lungs on imaging supports the possibility of an inflammatory lesion.
opposing_evidence: Body temperature 36.8℃, no fever
PCT 0.11 ng/ml, not supportive of significant severe bacterial infection
On physical examination, no dry or wet rales were heard in either lung, lacking typical auscultatory signs of pneumonia.
Severe hypercapnia (pCO2 76 mmHg↑) is relatively more prominent, and mild imaging abnormalities alone may not be sufficient to fully explain it.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute pulmonary embolism
supporting_evidence: Chest tightness and shortness of breath with acute onset for 4 days, worsening for 2 days
Respiratory rate 36 breaths/min, pulse 103 beats/min, with respiratory distress and tachycardia
At the outside hospital, “pulmonary embolism? heart failure?” had previously been considered in the differential diagnosis.
Elevated troponin (outside hospital troponin 154 pg/ml↑; admission TNT 109.7 pg/ml), which can be seen in acute pulmonary embolism with right heart strain or myocardial injury
Inability to lie flat at night suggests marked dyspnea; potentially fatal cardiopulmonary disease must be considered.
opposing_evidence: Arterial blood gas did not show typical hypocapnia; instead, it showed marked hypercapnia (pCO2 76 mmHg↑).
The chest CT report text and images further suggest linear opacities and a small amount of ground-glass opacity in both lungs, without providing definite direct evidence of pulmonary artery embolism.
No edema in both lower extremities; signs of deep vein thrombosis were not provided in the first stage
BNP 63 pg/ml, not elevated, with no obvious evidence of right heart failure
The ECG showed sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy, and nonspecific ST-T changes; no typical findings of right heart strain were provided.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute left heart failure/cardiogenic pulmonary edema
supporting_evidence: Progressive worsening of chest tightness and shortness of breath, and “unable to lie flat at night, requiring a seated forward-leaning position to rest,” consistent with orthopnea
History of hypertension for more than 10 years
Electrocardiogram (Figure 1) suggested "left ventricular hypertrophy and nonspecific ST-T changes," supporting the possibility of chronic hypertensive cardiac changes.
Elevated troponin can be seen in acute decompensated heart failure with myocardial injury
At an outside hospital, differential diagnosis was performed for “heart failure?”
opposing_evidence: BNP 63 pg/ml, does not support overt acute heart failure
Physical examination: 'cardiac silhouette not enlarged'; no dry or wet rales heard in either lung; no edema in either lower extremity; lacking typical signs of increased volume load.
The chest CT description did not indicate typical diffuse pulmonary edema or large pleural effusion.
At the outside hospital, diuresis, vasodilator therapy, and treatment to improve ventilation were given, with no improvement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute coronary syndrome or acute myocardial injury
supporting_evidence: At an outside hospital, troponin was 154 pg/ml↑; on admission, TNT was 109.7 pg/ml, and CK-MB was elevated at 39.6 U/L.
Chest tightness and shortness of breath may be atypical manifestations of acute coronary syndrome, especially in female patients.
History of hypertension for more than 10 years, a cardiovascular risk factor
ECG (Figure 1) shows "nonspecific ST-T changes"
opposing_evidence: Typical persistent chest pain or radiating pain was not described in the first stage
ECG showed only sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy, and nonspecific ST-T changes, with no definite features of acute ischemia provided
Symptoms are predominantly dyspnea and hypercapnia, suggesting that the mechanism of respiratory failure is more prominent.
BNP 63 pg/ml, cardiac silhouette not enlarged, no obvious evidence of acute pump failure

differential_diagnoses.name: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or acute decompensation of other obstructive ventilatory dysfunction
supporting_evidence: Marked hypercapnia (pCO2 76 mmHg↑) and acidosis (pH 7.29) suggest ventilatory failure.
Breath sounds in both lungs are slightly decreased, a physical sign that may be seen in obstructive ventilatory impairment
Exertional dyspnea worsened; during the acute phase, respiratory rate was 36 breaths/min
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, no chronic cough, sputum production, smoking history, or prior history of COPD/asthma was provided.
On physical examination, no wheezing was heard and there was no obvious prolongation of expiration.
The chest CT report and images did not indicate typical emphysema; instead, they showed multiple linear opacities and a small amount of ground-glass opacity in both lower lungs.
History of snoring, intermittent sleep apnea, and being overweight further supports a background of sleep-related hypoventilation

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Repeat bedside ECG showed further ST-segment depression in lead V4 compared with the previous tracing.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 51-year-old woman with progressively worsening chest tightness and dyspnea. She has a past history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Troponin and CK-MB were elevated before and after admission, and on Day +2 her condition acutely deteriorated, with tachycardia, worsening precordial chest tightness before loss of consciousness. At this time, it is first necessary to rapidly assess whether there is dyspnea and a circulatory event caused by acute myocardial ischemia, malignant arrhythmia, or acute coronary syndrome. A bedside ECG can be completed rapidly when the condition is unstable and noninvasive ventilatory support is required, to compare dynamic ST-T changes, determine whether immediate management as an acute coronary event is needed, and provide a basis for whether urgent coronary angiography should subsequently be performed; it also helps distinguish a cardiogenic cause from the subsequently identified neuromuscular respiratory failure.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Repeat myocardial enzyme testing showed that CK, CK-MB, TNT, etc. were all slightly decreased compared with the previous results.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At the initial presentation, the patient had chest tightness, dyspnea, elevated troponin and CK-MB, along with ECG changes and loss of consciousness during the acute exacerbation. Clinically, it is essential to dynamically assess whether there is progressive myocardial injury, acute myocardial infarction, or myocarditis. The core purpose of repeat cardiac enzyme testing is to observe whether the injury markers continue to rise, show a new peak, or begin to decline, thereby helping to determine whether the chest tightness and dyspnea are mainly caused by myocardial ischemia. In this case, repeat testing showed a slight decrease compared with the previous values, suggesting that it is not fully consistent with a typical progressive acute myocardial infarction. This is crucial for narrowing the differential diagnosis, avoiding attributing all symptoms to heart disease, and instead continuing to search for causes of hypercapnia and respiratory muscle weakness that cannot be explained by cardiopulmonary disease.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Urgent coronary and pulmonary angiography was performed.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient developed further ST-segment depression in lead V4 on the basis of chest tightness and dyspnea. Given the history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia and the elevation of myocardial injury markers, followed by sudden severe hypoxemia, bradycardia, loss of consciousness, and the need for chest compressions during defecation, this was a situation requiring urgent evaluation for life-threatening cardiovascular causes. Coronary angiography can directly determine whether there is a culprit vessel causing acute ischemia, the degree of stenosis, and distal blood flow, and is one of the most direct examinations for confirming or excluding acute coronary syndrome; it also determines whether interventional treatment is needed. In this case, angiography confirmed the presence of coronary artery disease, but no acute occlusive lesion was seen that could fully explain all manifestations of respiratory failure. Therefore, it completed the assessment of dangerous cardiac causes and also provided important exclusionary evidence for the subsequent consideration of myasthenia gravis-related respiratory muscle weakness.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Urgent coronary and pulmonary angiography was performed.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At disease onset, the patient presented with acute chest tightness and dyspnea and was considered at an outside hospital to have pulmonary embolism. During the course of illness, critical changes occurred, including a sudden drop in SpO2, loss of consciousness, and heart rate that first accelerated and then slowed. Clinically, acute pulmonary vascular embolism, a cause that can lead to sudden death, had to be excluded. Although prior data, including D-dimer and lower-extremity deep venous ultrasound, did not support this, direct further assessment of the pulmonary arteries was still required when the condition suddenly deteriorated. The purpose of pulmonary artery angiography was to determine whether there was a pulmonary arterial filling defect, explain the acute hypoxemia and risk of circulatory collapse, and guide whether thrombolysis, escalation of anticoagulation, or other management was needed. In this case, pulmonary artery angiography showed no abnormality, strongly excluding pulmonary embolism as the primary cause and shifting the diagnostic approach from acute cardiopulmonary emergencies toward neuromuscular respiratory failure.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Arterial blood gas was not obtained during transport; after transfer back to the ward, the blood gas analysis results were approximately the same as before, indicating a mildly elevated pCO2 of 50 mmHg.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At the time of admission, the patient already had significant type II respiratory failure, with pCO2 as high as 76 mmHg. During the course of illness, dyspnea worsened multiple times and improved after adjustment of noninvasive ventilation, suggesting that ventilatory impairment rather than isolated oxygenation impairment was more prominent. During emergency angiography and transport, the patient again developed dyspnea and a decrease in SpO2, making it necessary to reassess carbon dioxide retention, oxygenation status, and acid-base balance by blood gas analysis, in order to determine whether hypercapnia is still predominant, whether noninvasive ventilation is sufficient, and whether there is an indication for intubation. This test can also help analyze why the condition cannot be fully explained by coronary heart disease, pulmonary embolism, or mild pulmonary infection, because if imaging and cardiac evidence are limited while hypercapnia persists, a neuromuscular cause such as respiratory muscle weakness should be strongly suspected.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: At this time, we considered a neuromuscular disease and therefore requested a Neurology consultation.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After coronary angiography and pulmonary angiography, the patient’s chest tightness, dyspnea, and hypercapnia still could not be fully explained by cardiopulmonary disease; meanwhile, there were several key clinical clues: orthopnea on admission, strong dependence on BiPAP, several episodes of marked worsening of dyspnea that improved after ventilator adjustment, pulmonary physical findings that were never prominent, and on further questioning, choking with drinking water, dysphagia, dysarthria, and difficulty lifting the head. These manifestations suggest the possibility of involvement of the respiratory muscles, bulbar-innervated muscle groups, or the neuromuscular junction. The purpose of the neurology consultation was to perform a targeted neurologic examination and localization analysis, propose differential diagnostic considerations such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, and cerebrovascular accident, and guide the selection of subsequent tests such as lumbar puncture, electromyography, repetitive nerve stimulation, and antibody testing, which is crucial for establishing the etiology as quickly as possible and initiating immunotherapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The patient and family refused lumbar puncture.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At the time the patient developed dyspnea, the neurologic examination indicated dysarthria, limited assessment of the gag reflex, and decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes in all four extremities, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis, and cerebrovascular accident needed to be differentiated. Among these, Guillain-Barré syndrome can involve the respiratory muscles and lead to acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, and cerebrospinal fluid examination is of important value for identifying albuminocytologic dissociation and supporting or refuting this diagnosis. Ordering a lumbar puncture was primarily intended to address the key question of whether respiratory muscle weakness was caused by acute inflammatory peripheral neuropathy, which would in turn affect whether to continue immunoglobulin therapy and whether more aggressive airway management and neurologic intensive care monitoring were needed. Although the patient and family refused, the examination itself was a key part of the differential diagnostic workup at that time.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Promptly complete further examinations: electromyography: a large number of spontaneous potentials were seen in the left first dorsal interosseous, abductor pollicis brevis, and biceps brachii; please correlate clinically, and repeat examination is recommended;
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has type II respiratory failure that cannot be explained by common cardiopulmonary diseases, accompanied by dysphagia, dysarthria, neck muscle involvement, and decreased limb reflexes, making it necessary to further seek evidence from the neuromuscular perspective. Electromyography can assess patterns of involvement of the peripheral nerves, muscles, and neuromuscular junction, helping differentiate among myasthenia gravis, peripheral neuropathy, myopathy, or motor neuron disease at different lesion levels. In this case, the purpose of ordering electromyography is not only to verify the clinical inference of 'respiratory muscle weakness,' but also to provide a basis for whether repetitive nerve stimulation, immunotherapy, and long-term neurology follow-up will be needed subsequently. Although the current results are mainly spontaneous potentials, they still need to be interpreted in conjunction with the clinical findings and repeat testing is recommended, but they have further focused the diagnosis toward a neuromuscular disease.

recommended_exams.exam: Low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) (left trapezius muscle)
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) of the left trapezius muscle showed a decremental response.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has manifestations of bulbar muscle involvement (coughing/choking while drinking water, dysphagia, dysarthria) and respiratory muscle weakness, and also shows a marked response to neostigmine; clinically, myasthenia gravis is highly suspected. Low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation is a key electrophysiologic test for evaluating neuromuscular junction transmission function, especially when myasthenia gravis is suspected, and can provide objective evidence by observing whether there is a decrement in compound muscle action potential amplitude. Selecting proximal muscle groups such as the left trapezius is also consistent with the clinical characteristics of involvement of bulbar muscles, neck muscles, and respiration-related muscle groups in this case. The role of this test is to support the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis, reduce the uncertainty of drawing conclusions based solely on treatment response, and differentiate it from Guillain-Barre syndrome, primary myopathy, and other conditions.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody 8 nmol/L (+) (reference value < 0.04 nmol/L).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: During the course of the disease, involvement of the respiratory muscles, swallowing muscles, and muscles related to articulation was gradually established, and the neostigmine test was positive, while electrophysiologic studies suggested abnormal neuromuscular junction transmission; therefore, further immunologic evidence is needed to confirm myasthenia gravis. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody is one of the most important specific laboratory tests for adult myasthenia gravis. The purpose of this test is to confirm, at the level of pathophysiologic mechanism, an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder and to help differentiate it from functional symptoms, isolated sleep hypoventilation, post-infectious fatigue, and other peripheral neuromuscular disorders. This result is निर्णative for the final diagnosis, subsequent use of cholinesterase inhibitors and immunotherapy, and assessment of relapse and long-term management strategy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Sleep respiratory monitoring: does not meet criteria for sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome; nocturnal sleep-related hypoxemia (mild).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is overweight and has a history of snoring and intermittent sleep apnea. Early after admission, he also manifested marked hypercapnia, so obesity hypoventilation syndrome or obstructive sleep apnea did initially need to be considered as the primary etiology. However, as the course progressed, the patient developed choking with drinking water, dysphagia, dysarthria, difficulty lifting the head, and marked dependence on BiPAP. These manifestations suggest that a simple sleep-disordered breathing disorder cannot explain the entire clinical picture. The purpose of ordering sleep respiratory monitoring was to exclude the sleep-related hypoventilation that had previously been most likely to mislead the diagnostic direction, clarify its degree of contribution to the current type II respiratory failure, and provide counterevidence for ultimately attributing the etiology to neuromuscular respiratory failure; it could also assess nocturnal hypoxemia and provide a reference for the respiratory support plan.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Connective tissue disease-related: autoimmune hepatitis: anti-ENA antibody-3E (BPO) antigen (+), anti-ENA antibody-PML antigen (+); anti-ENA: anti-M2 antibody (+); rheumatoid factor, antiphospholipid antibodies, antinuclear antibody, vasculitis panel, and ANCA all (-).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease. The patient also has neuromuscular symptoms of unclear cause and mild liver function abnormalities. Clinically, it is necessary to assess whether there are other coexisting autoimmune abnormalities or an underlying systemic connective tissue disease so as not to miss comorbidities that could affect etiologic interpretation and subsequent treatment selection. The core clinical questions of this evaluation include: whether there is a concomitant systemic autoimmune disease, vasculitis, or other immune-mediated disease; whether these abnormalities can explain some of the neuromuscular manifestations or laboratory abnormalities; and whether, when immunotherapy is being considered, there is an immunologic background that requires concurrent evaluation and follow-up. Although the results did not support typical systemic vasculitis or common connective tissue diseases, they remain meaningful for completing the autoimmune profile and for long-term management.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Repeat chest CT showed absorption of the exudative lesions.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At disease onset, the patient developed chest tightness and shortness of breath after exposure to cold, with elevated inflammatory markers. The initial chest CT showed linear opacities in both lungs and small amounts of ground-glass opacities in the bilateral lower lungs, and community-acquired pneumonia or other infectious lesions had been considered; however, the severity of the dyspnea and carbon dioxide retention were not proportionate to the pulmonary imaging findings. The purpose of repeat lung CT was to dynamically assess whether the pulmonary exudative lesions had been absorbed, thereby determining the weight of infection in the overall condition, excluding progressive pulmonary parenchymal lesions as the cause of persistent respiratory failure, and verifying the clinical inference that 'the pulmonary lesions were not the primary pathogenic factor.' In this case, the repeat examination showed absorption of the exudative lesions, which helped explain the improvement in the pulmonary problem after anti-infective treatment, whereas the true dominant cause of the severe ventilatory failure was respiratory muscle involvement due to myasthenia gravis.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text:
At 11:30 on Day +2, the patient's chest tightness worsened compared with before. Physical examination: HR 132 beats/min, R 31 breaths/min, BP 135/76 mmHg, SpO2 94% (BiPAP), clear consciousness, tachypnea, no rales in the lungs. A bedside ECG showed further ST-segment depression in lead V4 compared with previously. Repeat cardiac enzyme testing (CK, CK-MB, TNT, etc., all slightly decreased compared with previously) was performed. Sublingual nitroglycerin was given without effect.
At 12:04, while defecating in bed, the patient developed sudden tachycardia and emotional agitation, followed by loss of consciousness, no response to calling, inability to trigger the ventilator spontaneously, cyanosis of the lips and fingertips, and SpO2 54%. Bag-assisted ventilation was immediately provided and oxygen flow was increased to 10 L/min. Thirty seconds later, the patient's heart rate rapidly decreased to 49 beats/min (without obvious ventricular fibrillation or premature ventricular contractions), SpO2 was unmeasurable, bilateral pupils were equal and round, diameter 2 mm, light reflex sluggish, and cyanosis of the lips worsened. Chest compressions were started immediately. At 12:06, the patient's spontaneous rhythm returned, and at 12:45, consciousness recovered. Emergency coronary angiography and pulmonary angiography were performed. Results: scattered plaques were seen in the left anterior descending coronary artery, with 60% focal stenosis in the proximal segment; scattered plaques were seen in the diagonal branch, with TIMI grade 3 distal flow; 80% focal stenosis was seen at the ostium, with TIMI grade 3 distal flow; no plaques or stenosis were seen in the remaining vessels. Pulmonary angiography showed no abnormality. At 15:00, after angiography, the patient was transferred back to the ward. During transport, dyspnea worsened again, accompanied by a decrease in SpO2. Oxygen flow was increased and the noninvasive ventilator was adjusted, after which dyspnea improved slightly. Arterial blood gas was not obtained during transport. After return to the ward, blood gas analysis was roughly similar to before, showing mildly elevated pCO2 of 50 mmHg.
Based on the above test results, coronary artery disease could be confirmed. However, after carefully reviewing the patient's clinical data, we found that the patient's chest tightness and dyspnea could not be explained by cardiopulmonary disease. At admission, the patient had obvious orthopnea, and symptoms improved with noninvasive ventilation, but the patient strongly refused removal of the noninvasive ventilator mask. During hospitalization, several episodes of marked worsening dyspnea also improved with ventilator adjustment, suggesting possible respiratory muscle weakness. At this point, we considered a neuromuscular disorder and requested a neurology consultation.
On further history-taking, the patient had one episode of choking while drinking water on Day -1, and did not eat afterward until nasogastric tube feeding was started after admission. Specialist examination: alert, slurred speech, pupils equal and round bilaterally, brisk light reflexes, extraocular movements intact, forceful eye closure, symmetric nasolabial folds, tongue protruded midline, pharyngeal reflex could not be assessed because oxygenation dropped immediately upon removal of the noninvasive ventilator mask, neck supple, muscle strength grade 4+ in all four extremities, decreased tendon reflex in the right upper extremity, tendon reflexes absent in the left upper extremity and both lower extremities, pathologic signs (-).
At this time, we considered that the patient had dysphagia and dysarthria, and that the dyspnea required exclusion of: 1. Guillain-Barre syndrome? 2. Myasthenia gravis? 3. Cerebrovascular accident? The patient and family refused lumbar puncture, so IVIG was given. After IVIG infusion, chest tightness and dyspnea improved slightly, and BiPAP could be paused for 2 minutes. Neostigmine 1.0 mg was given by intramuscular injection. Half an hour later, the dyspnea improved significantly, and after discontinuation of BiPAP there was no obvious chest tightness or dyspnea. This indicated a positive neostigmine test, and myasthenia gravis was considered the diagnosis. Pyridostigmine 60 mg Tid and IVIG (10 g/d x 5 days) were continued. Because levofloxacin was considered to carry a risk of worsening myasthenia, it was discontinued. After treatment, chest tightness and dyspnea improved markedly, and BiPAP was needed for only 3 hours per day; dysphagia improved significantly, and the patient could eat independently; dysarthria improved significantly, and speech and intonation returned to normal, allowing normal communication. To verify the final conclusion, we again reviewed the history. At disease onset, the patient had symptoms of pharyngeal muscle involvement, including choking while drinking water, dysphagia, and dysarthria, as well as neck muscle involvement with difficulty lifting the head, but without an obvious pattern of milder symptoms in the morning and worse symptoms in the evening. Further examinations were completed promptly: EMG: abundant spontaneous potentials were seen in the left first dorsal interosseous, abductor pollicis brevis, and biceps brachii; please correlate clinically and repeat testing was recommended. RNS (left trapezius): decrement was seen with low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody 8 nmol/L (+) (reference value < 0.04 nmol/L). Sleep respiratory monitoring: not consistent with sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome; nocturnal sleep hypoxemia (mild). Connective tissue disease-related tests: autoimmune liver panel: anti-ENA antibody-3E (BPO) antigen (+), anti-ENA antibody-PML antigen (+); anti-ENA: anti-M2 antibody (+); rheumatoid factor, antiphospholipid antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, vasculitis three-item panel, and ANCA were all (-). Repeat lung CT showed absorption of the exudative lesions.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis (type III, severe aggressive type), type II respiratory failure
diagnostic_basis: Symptoms: acute onset of chest tightness and dyspnea, with manifestations of respiratory muscle weakness; subsequent questioning revealed coughing/choking on drinking water, dysphagia, dysarthria, symptoms of pharyngeal/laryngeal muscle involvement, and difficulty lifting the head as a manifestation of neck muscle involvement.
Physical signs: orthopneic position, cardiopulmonary physical findings were generally normal

Ancillary examinations: ① neostigmine test (+); ② electromyography: a large number of spontaneous potentials were seen in the left first dorsal interosseous, abductor pollicis brevis, and biceps brachii; low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) (left trapezius) showed a decremental response; ③ anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody 8 nmol/L (+)

treatment_plan: Amlodipine for blood pressure lowering, rosuvastatin for lipid lowering, low-molecular-weight heparin sodium for anticoagulation, magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate for liver protection, regulation of the intestinal flora, indwelling nasogastric tube for enteral nutrition, symptomatic and supportive treatment
treatment_response: Chest tightness and shortness of breath significantly improved; BiPAP is only needed for 3 hours daily
Dysphagia significantly improved; able to eat independently
Dysarthria markedly improved; speech and intonation returned to normal, and the patient is able to communicate normally.
